data.title: Project Brief: Migrate Team Wiki to PlexiiWrite

content.text: Goals
Replace the current team wiki platform with PlexiiWrite to improve content accessibility, collaboration, and version control.
Enhance real-time editing capabilities to support faster decision-making and reduce meeting time spent on documentation.
Ensure all existing knowledge base content is fully migrated, preserved, and searchable within the new system.
Establish a standardized workflow for creating, reviewing, and publishing documentation across teams.
Scope
Full migration of all existing wiki pages, including project updates, process documents, and FAQs.
Configuration of user roles, permissions, and access controls to match current organizational structure.
Integration of key team workflows (e.g., approval chains, comment threads) into PlexiiWrite’s native features.
Training sessions for all team members on using the new platform effectively.
Exclusion of external tools or third-party integrations not directly tied to content management.
Timeline
Week 1–2
: Finalize content inventory, define migration criteria, and set up PlexiiWriten environment.
Week 3–4
: Begin content migration; validate accuracy and formatting.
Week 5
: Conduct internal testing with cross-functional teams; gather feedback.
Week 6
: Launch phased rollout to departments; provide ongoing support.
Week 7
: Complete full adoption; conduct post-migration review.
Risks
Content loss or formatting errors during migration due to platform differences.
Resistance from users accustomed to the current wiki interface or workflow.
Delays in user adoption if training materials are insufficient or not timely.

# Onboarding Guide for New Support Agents – First Week

## Welcome and Orientation

Welcome to the support team! This guide is designed to help you get up to speed during your first week. You’ll be introduced to key tools, processes, and protocols that ensure consistent, efficient, and customer-focused support.

Your first week will focus on understanding our systems, learning how to handle common issues, and familiarizing yourself with escalation procedures. The goal is to build confidence in your ability to resolve tickets independently while knowing when and how to escalate appropriately.

---

## Week 1: Key Tools and Systems

You will be assigned a dedicated onboarding manager who will walk you through each system. Below are the core tools you’ll use daily:

- **Zendesk** – Our primary ticketing platform. Use it to log, track, and respond to customer inquiries. Learn to:
  - Create new tickets using standard templates.
  - Search for existing cases using keywords and filters.
  - Assign tickets to team members or escalate as needed.
  - Update ticket status and add notes for clarity.

- **CRM (Salesforce)** – Used to view customer profiles, purchase history, and service interactions. You will:
  - Access customer data securely to provide personalized support.
  - Log all interactions directly into the CRM to maintain a complete service record.

- **Internal Knowledge Base (Confluence)** – A central repository of FAQs, troubleshooting steps, and best practices. You will:
  - Search by topic or keyword to find solutions.
  - Bookmark frequently used articles for quick access.
  - Report outdated or missing content to your manager.

- **Slack** – The team communication hub. Use it to:
  - Join relevant channels (e.g., #support-general, #onboarding, #escalations).
  - Ask questions in real time.
  - Receive alerts on urgent tickets or escalations.

- **Google Workspace (Docs & Sheets)** – Used for internal tracking and documentation. You’ll access:
  - Weekly performance dashboards.
  - Shared checklists for onboarding tasks and escalation reviews.

---

## Handling Customer Tickets: Step-by-Step

When a customer reaches out:

1. **Acknowledge promptly** – Respond within one minute of receiving a ticket.
2. **Categorize the issue** – Use Zendesk’s tagging system to classify by type (e.g., billing, technical, account access).

# Weekly Product Review Meeting Notes

## Meeting Date  
[Insert Date]

## Attendees  
[List names and roles, e.g., Alex Chen – Product Manager, Sam Rivera – UX Designer, Jordan Lee – Engineering Lead]

---

## Agenda Items

### 1. Pricing Page  
- Current state: The pricing page has been updated with new tier options, including a free trial plan.  
- User feedback: Early tests show mixed reactions—some users find the tier comparisons confusing due to lack of visual hierarchy.  
- Action items:  
  - Redesign tier comparison section with clearer icons and side-by-side visuals (due: [insert date]).  
  - Add tooltips explaining value propositions for each tier (due: [insert date]).  
  - A/B test two versions of the page (current vs. redesigned) over the next two weeks (due: [insert date]).

### 2. Onboarding Drop-Off  
- Data summary: 42% of new users drop off during the second step of onboarding (after initial setup).  
- Root causes identified:  
  - Step requires user to input personal information early, which feels intrusive.  
  - Lack of progress indicators makes users unsure if they’re making progress.  
- Action items:  
  - Delay personal info collection until after user completes core feature exploration (due: [insert date]).  
  - Add a progress bar and brief tooltips at each step to improve perceived flow (due: [insert date]).  
  - Run a short usability test with 10 new users next week to validate changes (due: [insert date]).

### 3. Mobile Beta  
- Current status: Beta version launched to 500 users on iOS and Android.  
- Key feedback:  
  - Users report slow load times on low-end devices.  
  - Navigation is inconsistent across screen sizes.  
- Action items:  
  - Optimize image loading and reduce bundle size by 25% (due: [insert date]).  
  - Realign navigation structure to follow a consistent pattern across platforms (due: [insert date]).  
  - Schedule a follow-up feedback session with beta testers next week to gather specific pain points (due: [insert date]).

---

## Next Steps & Ownership  
- Finalize pricing page redesign mockups by [insert date] – UX Team  
- Share onboarding drop-off data with marketing team for campaign adjustments – Product Manager  
- Compile mobile beta feedback report by [insert date] – Engineering Lead  

---

## Open Questions  
- Should we introduce a free tier with limited features to reduce friction in onboarding?  
- How should we balance feature completeness with performance in the mobile app?

---  
*Note: These notes will be shared with all product and engineering teams by end of day.*

data.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report

slides.title: Why Bug Reports Matter
bullets: Clear bug reports help developers fix issues faster
They reduce miscommunication and avoid rework
A well-written report saves time and improves team efficiency
Every bug is a chance to improve product quality
Good reports build trust between testers and engineers
Consistent reporting enables better tracking and analysis
slides.notes: Start by emphasizing that bug reports aren't just about finding errors—they're tools for collaboration. A clear, structured report helps everyone understand the problem and act on it quickly.

slides.title: The Core Elements of a Good Report
bullets: Describe what happens (steps to reproduce)
State exactly what is expected vs. what actually occurs
Include environment details: device, OS, browser, version
Attach screenshots or logs if available
Specify severity level: critical, high, medium, low
Keep language simple and objective
slides.notes: Every good report must have these key components. Focus on clarity and precision—avoid assumptions or emotional language. The goal is for anyone reading it to know exactly what went wrong and how to fix it.

slides.title: How to Reproduce the Issue
bullets: Start with a clear step-by-step sequence
Use numbered steps for readability
Ensure each step is specific and actionable
Include any required user actions or inputs
Verify that the issue occurs consistently under the same conditions
Note if the bug only appears under certain conditions
slides.notes: Reproducibility is critical. A tester should be able to follow the steps and see the bug without guessing. Be precise—don’t say 'sometimes' or 'after a while'.

slides.title: Avoiding Common Pitfalls
bullets: Never assume the bug is user error
Don't skip environment details
Avoid vague statements like 'it doesn't work'
Resist the urge to add opinions or guesses
Don't include unrelated information or screenshots
Double-check that all steps are complete and accurate
slides.notes: Common mistakes slow down fixes. Always ask: Is this report actionable? Can someone reproduce it with just the info provided? If not, go back and refine.

slides.title: Example: From Confusing to Clear
bullets: Bad: 'It broke when I clicked it.'
Good: 'After clicking the 'Save' button on the profile page, the screen freezes and shows a blank white screen. Expected behavior: save confirmation appears. OS: Windows 10, Browser: Chrome v120.'
slides.notes: This contrast shows how a simple rewrite transforms a vague complaint into a useful, actionable report. Use this as a real-world example to illustrate the impact of clarity.

slides.title: Next Steps & Ownership
bullets: Submit the report through the designated tool or system
Assign a developer or team member for follow-up
Confirm receipt and acknowledge the report
Track resolution status until closed
Use feedback to improve future reporting practices
slides.notes: Closing the loop is important. Make sure every report has a clear path from submission to resolution. Encourage team members to take ownership and stay engaged in the process.
